abstract: Despite the rise in employment, consistently high EU-average poverty rates continue to generate debates about the factors that explain the level and changes in the relative poverty rate, both within and across countries. Assuming a strong negative correlation between poverty and employment, the article investigates the role of four mechanisms responsible for this blurred relationship: changes in employment levels, the distribution of paid work between households, the within-household concentration of paid work, and the role of social transfers. The article shows that using a floating poverty threshold considerably underestimates the strength of the relationships between poverty, employment and social transfers.
summary_en: Why have EU poverty rates remained stubbornly high despite rising employment? Gábos, Binder, Branyiczki and Tóth use cross-country EU-SILC data to disentangle four mechanisms: changes in employment levels, between-household work distribution, within-household work concentration, and social-transfer adjustments. They show that using a floating (relative) poverty threshold — the standard EU practice — substantially understates the strength of the underlying poverty-employment-transfer relationships. The implication: standard EU poverty measurement underestimates how much policy actually moves the needle.
data_used: EU-SILC (Statistics on Income and Living Conditions) cross-country panel data covering all EU member states over multiple years, with detailed household income, employment, and social-transfer variables.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for KSH poverty-statistics methodology and Pénzügyminisztérium social-policy analysis. The paper supports complementing EU floating-threshold poverty measures with anchored-threshold variants when assessing the impact of Hungarian social-transfer reforms. Also relevant for the Equal Treatment Authority and EU DG-EMPL in evaluating poverty-reduction targets.
title: Unravelling the relationship between employment, social transfers and income poverty
